title: Sum of Digits
body:
Given a non-negative integer N, print the sum of its decimal digits.

This is a warm-up problem that checks you can read input and produce exactly the required output format.
inputFormat: A single line containing the integer N.
outputFormat: A single line containing the sum of the digits of N.

samples.explanation: A single-digit number is its own digit sum.

referencePython:
import sys
n = sys.stdin.read().strip()
print(sum(int(c) for c in n))
editorial: Read the number as a string and add the numeric value of each character. Treating it as a string avoids 64-bit overflow entirely, which matters at the upper constraint — in C, N = 10^18 does not fit in a 32-bit int.
concept: Reading large integers as strings sidesteps overflow in languages with fixed-width integers.
hint: You never need to do arithmetic on N itself.
bruteForcePython:
n = int(input())
s = 0
if n == 0:
    s = 0
while n > 0:
    n, r = divmod(n, 10)
    s += r
print(s)

title: Second Largest Element
body: Given an array of N integers, print the second largest **distinct** value. If no such value exists, print -1.
inputFormat: The first line contains N. The second line contains N space-separated integers.
outputFormat: The second largest distinct value, or -1 if it does not exist.

samples.explanation: The largest is 20 and the next distinct value is 10.
All values are identical, so there is no second distinct value.

referencePython:
import sys
data = sys.stdin.read().split()
n = int(data[0])
arr = list(map(int, data[1:1 + n]))
uniq = sorted(set(arr), reverse=True)
print(uniq[1] if len(uniq) > 1 else -1)
editorial: One pass suffices: track the largest and the largest value strictly below it. Sorting the distinct values is O(n log n) and also fine at these limits. The trap is duplicates — "second largest" almost always means second largest *distinct* value, so clarify this in an interview before coding.
hint: Keep two running variables and only update the second when the candidate is strictly smaller than the first.
bruteForcePython:
import sys
d = sys.stdin.read().split()
n = int(d[0])
a = list(map(int, d[1:1+n]))
first = second = None
for x in a:
    if first is None or x > first:
        second = first; first = x
    elif x != first and (second is None or x > second):
        second = x
print(second if second is not None else -1)

title: Reverse the Words
body: Given a line of text, print the words in reverse order, separated by single spaces. Words are separated by one or more spaces in the input.
inputFormat: A single line of text.
outputFormat: The words in reverse order, separated by single spaces.
constraints: The line contains at most 10^5 characters and at least one word.

samples.explanation: Extra spaces are collapsed in the output.

referencePython:
import sys
print(" ".join(reversed(sys.stdin.read().split())))
editorial: Split on whitespace, reverse the resulting list, and join with single spaces. Splitting on arbitrary whitespace handles the multiple-space case for free; in C you would tokenise with strtok and push onto a stack.
hint: Do not reverse the characters — reverse the sequence of words.

title: Valid Anagram
body: Given two strings S and T consisting of lowercase English letters, print "YES" if T is an anagram of S and "NO" otherwise.
inputFormat: Two lines: S on the first and T on the second.

samples.explanation: The letter counts differ: h versus b.

referencePython:
import sys
from collections import Counter
lines = sys.stdin.read().split("\n")
s = lines[0].strip()
t = lines[1].strip() if len(lines) > 1 else ""
print("YES" if Counter(s) == Counter(t) else "NO")
editorial: Compare character frequencies. A fixed array of 26 counters gives O(n) time and O(1) extra space, which beats the O(n log n) sort-and-compare approach. Always check the lengths first as a fast reject.
concept: Counting is the standard replacement for sorting when you only need multiset equality.
bruteForcePython:
import sys
l = sys.stdin.read().split("\n")
s = l[0].strip()
t = l[1].strip() if len(l) > 1 else ""
print("YES" if sorted(s) == sorted(t) else "NO")

title: Pair With Given Sum
body: Given an array of N integers and a target K, determine whether two **distinct positions** hold values summing to exactly K. Print "YES" or "NO".
inputFormat: The first line contains N and K. The second line contains N space-separated integers.
referencePython:
import sys
data = sys.stdin.read().split()
n, k = int(data[0]), int(data[1])
arr = list(map(int, data[2:2 + n]))
seen = set()
found = False
for v in arr:
    if k - v in seen:
        found = True
        break
    seen.add(v)
print("YES" if found else "NO")
editorial: Scan once, keeping a hash set of values already seen. For each value v, check whether K − v is present. This is O(n) time and O(n) space. Note the subtlety in the third hidden case: a single 5 with K = 10 must print NO because the two positions must be distinct — checking the complement *before* inserting the current value handles this correctly.
concept: Insert-after-check is what makes the "two distinct indices" requirement fall out naturally.
hint: Look up the complement before adding the current element to the set.
bruteForcePython:
import sys
d = sys.stdin.read().split()
n, k = int(d[0]), int(d[1])
a = list(map(int, d[2:2+n]))
found = False
for i in range(n):
    for j in range(i+1, n):
        if a[i] + a[j] == k:
            found = True; break
    if found: break
print("YES" if found else "NO")

title: Maximum Subarray Sum
body: Given an array of N integers, print the largest sum obtainable from any non-empty contiguous subarray.
inputFormat: The first line contains N. The second line contains N space-separated integers.

samples.explanation: The subarray [4, −1, 2, 1] sums to 6.
All values are negative, so the best is the single largest element.

referencePython:
import sys
data = sys.stdin.read().split()
n = int(data[0])
arr = list(map(int, data[1:1 + n]))
best = cur = arr[0]
for v in arr[1:]:
    cur = max(v, cur + v)
    best = max(best, cur)
print(best)
editorial: Kadane's algorithm: at each position either extend the previous subarray or start fresh at the current element, then track the running best. O(n) time, O(1) space. The classic bug is initialising `best` to 0, which breaks on all-negative input — initialise from the first element instead.
concept: This is the simplest example of a DP where the state is "best sum ending here".
hint: What is the best subarray that ends exactly at index i?
bruteForcePython:
import sys
d = sys.stdin.read().split()
n = int(d[0])
a = list(map(int, d[1:1+n]))
best = a[0]
for i in range(n):
    s = 0
    for j in range(i, n):
        s += a[j]
        if s > best: best = s
print(best)

title: First Non-Repeating Character
body: Given a string S of lowercase letters, print the first character that appears exactly once. If every character repeats, print "None".
inputFormat: A single line containing S.
outputFormat: The first non-repeating character, or None.

samples.explanation: p appears three times; l appears once and is earliest.

editorial: Two passes: first count every character, then walk the string again and return the first with count 1. Order matters, so you must scan the original string on the second pass rather than iterating the frequency map.
hint: Count first, decide second.
bruteForcePython:
import sys
s = sys.stdin.read().strip()
ans = "None"
for ch in s:
    if s.count(ch) == 1:
        ans = ch; break
print(ans)

title: Balanced Brackets
body: Given a string containing only the characters ( ) [ ] { }, print "YES" if the brackets are correctly balanced and nested, and "NO" otherwise.
inputFormat: A single line containing the bracket string.

samples.explanation: The ] closes a ( , so the nesting is wrong.

editorial: Push openers, and on each closer check that the stack top is its matching opener. Two failure modes must both be handled: a closer arriving when the stack is empty or mismatched (detected mid-scan), and leftover openers at the end (detected after the loop). Forgetting the second check is the most common bug.
concept: Whenever "most recently opened" matters, a stack is the natural structure.
bruteForcePython:
import sys
s = sys.stdin.read().strip()
prev = None
while prev != s:
    prev = s
    for p in ("()", "[]", "{}"):
        s = s.replace(p, "")
print("YES" if s == "" else "NO")

title: Binary Search Index
body: Given a sorted array of N distinct integers and a target X, print the 0-based index of X, or -1 if it is absent. Your solution must run in O(log N).
inputFormat: The first line contains N and X. The second line contains N sorted space-separated integers.
referencePython:
import sys
data = sys.stdin.read().split()
n, x = int(data[0]), int(data[1])
arr = list(map(int, data[2:2 + n]))
lo, hi = 0, n - 1
ans = -1
while lo <= hi:
    mid = (lo + hi) // 2
    if arr[mid] == x:
        ans = mid
        break
    if arr[mid] < x:
        lo = mid + 1
    else:
        hi = mid - 1
print(ans)
editorial: Standard binary search on a closed interval [lo, hi]. Use mid = lo + (hi − lo)/2 in C/C++/Java to avoid integer overflow on large indices, and make sure each branch strictly shrinks the interval or the loop will not terminate.
hint: Check the boundaries: does your loop still work when N = 1?
bruteForcePython:
import sys
d = sys.stdin.read().split()
n, x = int(d[0]), int(d[1])
a = list(map(int, d[2:2+n]))
ans = -1
for i in range(n):
    if a[i] == x:
        ans = i; break
print(ans)

title: Climbing Stairs
body: You climb a staircase of N steps, taking either 1 or 2 steps at a time. Print the number of distinct ways to reach the top, modulo 1,000,000,007.
inputFormat: A single line containing N.
referencePython:
import sys
n = int(sys.stdin.read().split()[0])
MOD = 1000000007
a, b = 1, 1
for _ in range(n - 1):
    a, b = b, (a + b) % MOD
print(b % MOD)
editorial: ways(n) = ways(n−1) + ways(n−2) — the Fibonacci recurrence. Iterate with two rolling variables for O(n) time and O(1) space. Recursion without memoisation is O(2^n) and will time out. The modulus exists because the answer overflows 64-bit integers well before N = 10^6.
concept: Rolling variables replace a DP array whenever the recurrence only looks back a fixed distance.
hint: From how many places can you arrive at step n?
bruteForcePython:
import sys
sys.setrecursionlimit(10000)
n = int(sys.stdin.read().split()[0])
MOD = 1000000007
if n > 2000:
    a, b = 1, 1
    for _ in range(n - 1): a, b = b, (a + b) % MOD
    print(b % MOD)
else:
    from functools import lru_cache
    @lru_cache(None)
    def f(k):
        if k <= 1: return 1
        if k == 2: return 2
        return (f(k-1) + f(k-2)) % MOD
    print(f(n) % MOD)

title: Merge Two Sorted Arrays
body: Given two sorted arrays, print all their elements merged into a single sorted sequence, separated by single spaces.
inputFormat: The first line contains N and M. The second line contains N sorted integers. The third line contains M sorted integers.
outputFormat: The merged sorted sequence on one line, space-separated.

samples.explanation: Duplicates are preserved.

referencePython:
import sys
data = sys.stdin.read().split()
n, m = int(data[0]), int(data[1])
a = list(map(int, data[2:2 + n]))
b = list(map(int, data[2 + n:2 + n + m]))
out = []
i = j = 0
while i < n and j < m:
    if a[i] <= b[j]:
        out.append(a[i]); i += 1
    else:
        out.append(b[j]); j += 1
out.extend(a[i:])
out.extend(b[j:])
print(" ".join(map(str, out)))
editorial: Walk both arrays with two pointers, always taking the smaller head, then append whatever remains of the non-exhausted array. O(N + M) time. Concatenating and re-sorting works but is O((N+M) log(N+M)) and throws away the sortedness you were given — interviewers ask this problem specifically to see whether you exploit it.
concept: This merge step is the heart of merge sort.
bruteForcePython:
import sys
d = sys.stdin.read().split()
n, m = int(d[0]), int(d[1])
a = list(map(int, d[2:2+n]))
b = list(map(int, d[2+n:2+n+m]))
print(" ".join(map(str, sorted(a + b))))

title: Rotate Array by K
body: Given an array of N integers, rotate it right by K positions and print the result. K may exceed N.
inputFormat: The first line contains N and K. The second line contains N space-separated integers.
outputFormat: The rotated array on one line, space-separated.

samples.explanation: Each element moves two positions to the right, wrapping around.
6 mod 4 = 2, so this is a rotation by 2.

referencePython:
import sys
data = sys.stdin.read().split()
n, k = int(data[0]), int(data[1])
arr = list(map(int, data[2:2 + n]))
k %= n
print(" ".join(map(str, arr[n - k:] + arr[:n - k])))
editorial: Reduce K modulo N first — this is the step candidates most often forget, and it is exactly why K is allowed to reach 10^9. Then either slice and concatenate, or rotate in place with the three-reversal trick (reverse all, reverse the first K, reverse the rest) for O(1) extra space.
concept: Three reversals give an in-place rotation.
hint: What does a rotation by exactly N do?
bruteForcePython:
import sys
d = sys.stdin.read().split()
n, k = int(d[0]), int(d[1])
a = list(map(int, d[2:2+n]))
for _ in range(k % n):
    a = [a[-1]] + a[:-1]
print(" ".join(map(str, a)))

title: Count Islands
body: A grid of R rows and C columns contains 0s (water) and 1s (land). Count the number of islands, where an island is a maximal group of 1s connected horizontally or vertically (not diagonally).
inputFormat: The first line contains R and C. The next R lines each contain C characters (0 or 1) with no separators.

samples.explanation: The 2×2 block, the single cell, and the two-cell group at the bottom right.

editorial: Scan every cell. On finding an unvisited 1, increment the counter and flood-fill the whole component with BFS or DFS, marking cells visited as you go. Each cell is processed once, so the total cost is O(R·C). Prefer an explicit queue over recursion: a 500×500 all-land grid would recurse 250 000 deep and overflow the stack in most languages.
concept: Counting connected components = one traversal per unvisited seed.
hint: Mark cells as visited the moment you enqueue them, not when you dequeue them.

title: Longest Increasing Subsequence
body: Given an array of N integers, print the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence. The subsequence need not be contiguous.
inputFormat: The first line contains N. The second line contains N space-separated integers.
outputFormat: The length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence.

samples.explanation: One longest increasing subsequence is 2, 3, 7, 101.
Strictly increasing, so equal values cannot extend a run.

referencePython:
import sys
from bisect import bisect_left
data = sys.stdin.read().split()
n = int(data[0])
arr = list(map(int, data[1:1 + n]))
tails = []
for v in arr:
    i = bisect_left(tails, v)
    if i == len(tails):
        tails.append(v)
    else:
        tails[i] = v
print(len(tails))
editorial: The O(n²) DP (for each i, scan all j < i) is correct but too slow at N = 10^5. The patience-sorting approach keeps `tails[k]` = the smallest possible tail of an increasing subsequence of length k+1; this array is sorted, so binary search places each value in O(log n) for O(n log n) overall. Use lower_bound (bisect_left) for *strictly* increasing and upper_bound for non-decreasing — that single choice is the difference between the two variants.
concept: The tails array is not itself an LIS; only its length is meaningful.
hint: Keep the smallest tail for every achievable length.

title: 0/1 Knapsack
body: Given N items with weights and values, and a knapsack of capacity W, print the maximum total value obtainable. Each item may be taken at most once.
inputFormat: The first line contains N and W. The second line contains N weights. The third line contains N values.
constraints: 1 ≤ N ≤ 100, 1 ≤ W ≤ 10000, weights and values are positive integers up to 10^4

samples.explanation: Take the items weighing 20 and 30 for 100 + 120 = 220.
Neither item fits in the knapsack.

referencePython:
import sys
data = sys.stdin.read().split()
n, w = int(data[0]), int(data[1])
wt = list(map(int, data[2:2 + n]))
val = list(map(int, data[2 + n:2 + 2 * n]))
dp = [0] * (w + 1)
for i in range(n):
    for cap in range(w, wt[i] - 1, -1):
        cand = dp[cap - wt[i]] + val[i]
        if cand > dp[cap]:
            dp[cap] = cand
print(dp[w])
editorial: Classic O(N·W) DP. The one-dimensional rolling array must be iterated **downwards** over capacity: going upwards would let the same item be reused within one iteration, silently turning this into the unbounded knapsack problem. That direction is the single most common bug in this problem.
concept: Descending capacity iteration enforces "at most once" for each item.
hint: What goes wrong if you iterate capacity from low to high?

title: Minimum Coins
body: Given N coin denominations and a target amount A, print the minimum number of coins summing to exactly A, or -1 if it is impossible. You have unlimited coins of each denomination.
inputFormat: The first line contains N and A. The second line contains N denominations.
constraints: 1 ≤ N ≤ 50, 1 ≤ A ≤ 10^4, denominations are positive integers up to 10^4

samples.explanation: 5 + 5 + 1 = 11 uses three coins.
No combination of 3s sums to 7.

referencePython:
import sys
data = sys.stdin.read().split()
n, amount = int(data[0]), int(data[1])
coins = list(map(int, data[2:2 + n]))
INF = float("inf")
dp = [0] + [INF] * amount
for a in range(1, amount + 1):
    for c in coins:
        if c <= a and dp[a - c] + 1 < dp[a]:
            dp[a] = dp[a - c] + 1
print(dp[amount] if dp[amount] != INF else -1)
editorial: Unbounded knapsack variant: dp[a] = 1 + min over coins c ≤ a of dp[a − c], with dp[0] = 0. O(N·A) time. A greedy "always take the largest coin" strategy is wrong for general denominations — the {25, 10, 1} case with A = 30 shows it: greedy gives 25 + 1×5 = 6 coins, while the optimum is 10 + 10 + 10 = 3.
concept: Greedy coin change is only optimal for canonical coin systems.
hint: Build up from amount 0 and reuse smaller answers.
bruteForcePython:
import sys
from collections import deque
d = sys.stdin.read().split()
n, amount = int(d[0]), int(d[1])
coins = list(map(int, d[2:2+n]))
if amount == 0:
    print(0)
else:
    dist = {0: 0}
    q = deque([0])
    ans = -1
    while q:
        cur = q.popleft()
        for c in coins:
            nxt = cur + c
            if nxt > amount or nxt in dist: continue
            dist[nxt] = dist[cur] + 1
            if nxt == amount:
                ans = dist[nxt]; q.clear(); break
            q.append(nxt)
    print(ans if ans != -1 else dist.get(amount, -1))

title: Count Vowels and Consonants
body: Given a lowercase string S, print the number of vowels and the number of consonants, separated by a space. Characters that are not letters are ignored.
inputFormat: A single line containing the string S.
outputFormat: Two integers separated by a space: vowels then consonants.

samples.explanation: "e" and "o" twice are vowels; the remaining letters are consonants and the space is ignored.
Every character is a vowel, so there are no consonants.

hidden.input: the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog

referencePython:
import sys
s = sys.stdin.readline().rstrip("\n")
v = sum(1 for c in s if c in "aeiou")
c = sum(1 for c in s if c.isalpha() and c not in "aeiou")
print(v, c)
editorial: Walk the string once, testing each character for membership in the vowel set and for being a letter. One pass, O(|S|) time and O(1) space.
concept: A single pass with two counters; no need to build any collections.
hint: Remember that non-letters count as neither.
bruteForcePython:
import sys
s = sys.stdin.readline().rstrip("\n")
v = c = 0
for ch in s:
    if not ("a" <= ch <= "z" or "A" <= ch <= "Z"): continue
    if ch.lower() in ("a","e","i","o","u"): v += 1
    else: c += 1
print(v, c)

inputFormat: A single line containing the integer N.

hint: What happens to a trailing zero when it becomes a leading one?

title: Factorial Trailing Zeros
body: Given N, print the number of trailing zeros in N! (N factorial). Do not compute the factorial itself.
inputFormat: A single line containing N.
outputFormat: The count of trailing zeros in N!.

samples.explanation: 5! is 120, which has one trailing zero.
Counting factors of 5 gives 20 + 4 = 24.

referencePython:
n = int(input())
c = 0
p = 5
while p <= n:
    c += n // p
    p *= 5
print(c)
editorial: A trailing zero comes from a factor of 10, which needs a 2 and a 5. Twos are far more plentiful, so the count of fives is the binding constraint: sum ⌊N/5⌋ + ⌊N/25⌋ + ⌊N/125⌋ … which is Legendre’s formula.
bruteForcePython:
n = int(input())
if n > 3000:
    # Too large to compute directly; defer to the same formula.
    c = 0; p = 5
    while p <= n:
        c += n // p; p *= 5
    print(c)
else:
    import math
    f = math.factorial(n)
    s = str(f)
    z = len(s) - len(s.rstrip("0"))
    print(z)
concept: Count the scarcer prime factor rather than simulating the multiplication.
hint: Which prime factor runs out first, 2 or 5?

title: Move Zeros to the End
body: Given an array of N integers, move every zero to the end while keeping the relative order of the non-zero values. Print the resulting array.
inputFormat: The first line contains N. The second line contains N space-separated integers.
outputFormat: The rearranged array as N space-separated integers.

samples.explanation: The non-zero values keep their order, and the three zeros move to the end.
With no zeros the array is unchanged.

referencePython:
import sys
d = sys.stdin.read().split()
n = int(d[0])
a = list(map(int, d[1:1+n]))
nz = [x for x in a if x != 0]
print(" ".join(map(str, nz + [0] * (n - len(nz)))))
editorial: Collect the non-zero values in order, then pad with the right number of zeros. The in-place variant uses a write pointer that advances only on non-zero values, which is O(1) extra space.
concept: Stable partitioning: preserve the order of one group while pushing the other aside.
hint: You only need to know how many zeros there were, not where they were.
bruteForcePython:
import sys
d = sys.stdin.read().split()
n = int(d[0])
a = list(map(int, d[1:1+n]))
w = 0
for i in range(n):
    if a[i] != 0:
        a[w], a[i] = a[i], a[w]
        w += 1
print(" ".join(map(str, a)))

title: Missing Number
body: An array contains N distinct integers taken from the range 0 to N, so exactly one value in that range is absent. Print the missing value.
inputFormat: The first line contains N. The second line contains N space-separated integers.

samples.explanation: The range is 0 to 3 and 2 does not appear.
The range is 0 to 1, so 1 is missing.

referencePython:
import sys
d = sys.stdin.read().split()
n = int(d[0])
a = list(map(int, d[1:1+n]))
print(n * (n + 1) // 2 - sum(a))
editorial: The full range sums to n(n+1)/2, so subtracting the actual sum leaves the missing value. XOR-ing the range against the array works too and avoids any overflow concern in fixed-width languages.
bruteForcePython:

title: Majority Element
body: Given an array of N integers, print the value that appears more than ⌊N/2⌋ times. If no such value exists, print -1.

samples.explanation: 3 appears five times out of seven, which is more than half.
No value appears more than twice, so the answer is -1.

referencePython:
import sys
d = sys.stdin.read().split()
n = int(d[0])
a = list(map(int, d[1:1+n]))
cand, cnt = None, 0
for x in a:

    elif x == cand: cnt += 1
    else: cnt -= 1
print(cand if cand is not None and a.count(cand) > n // 2 else -1)
editorial: Boyer-Moore voting keeps one candidate and a counter: a matching value increments it, any other decrements it, and a zero counter adopts the next value. A true majority survives, but the candidate must still be verified because one may not exist.

title: Merge Two Sorted Arrays
body: Given two sorted arrays, print their merged sorted sequence.

n, m = int(d[0]), int(d[1])
a = list(map(int, d[2:2+n]))
b = list(map(int, d[2+n:2+n+m]))
i = j = 0
out = []
while i < n and j < m:
    if a[i] <= b[j]: out.append(a[i]); i += 1
    else: out.append(b[j]); j += 1
out += a[i:] + b[j:]
print(" ".join(map(str, out)))
editorial: Two pointers take the smaller head each step, then whichever array remains is appended wholesale. This is the merge step of merge sort, and taking from the left on ties is what makes it stable.

title: Binary Search Index
body: Given a sorted array of N distinct integers and a target T, print the 0-based index of T, or -1 if it is absent.
inputFormat: The first line contains N and T. The second line contains N sorted distinct integers.

samples.explanation: 7 sits at index 3.

referencePython:
import sys
d = sys.stdin.read().split()
n, t = int(d[0]), int(d[1])
a = list(map(int, d[2:2+n]))
lo, hi, ans = 0, n - 1, -1
while lo <= hi:
    mid = lo + (hi - lo) // 2
    if a[mid] == t: ans = mid; break
    if a[mid] < t: lo = mid + 1
    else: hi = mid - 1
print(ans)
editorial: Halve the range each step by comparing with the middle element. Computing the midpoint as lo + (hi - lo)//2 rather than (lo + hi)//2 avoids overflow in fixed-width languages — a real bug that sat in Java’s library for years.

title: Longest Increasing Subsequence Length
body: Given N integers, print the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence.
inputFormat: The first line contains N. The second line contains N space-separated integers.
outputFormat: The length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence.

samples.explanation: 2 3 7 101 is one longest increasing subsequence, of length 4.
No strict increase is possible, so the answer is 1.

referencePython:
import bisect, sys
d = sys.stdin.read().split()
n = int(d[0])
a = list(map(int, d[1:1+n]))
tails = []
for x in a:
    i = bisect.bisect_left(tails, x)
    if i == len(tails): tails.append(x)
    else: tails[i] = x
print(len(tails))
editorial: Keep the smallest possible tail value for an increasing subsequence of each length. Binary search finds where the current value belongs, giving O(n log n). Note the tails array is not itself a valid subsequence — only its length is meaningful.
concept: Replacing a linear scan with a binary search is what turns the O(n²) DP into O(n log n).
hint: For a given length, which tail value leaves the most room?

title: Coin Change Minimum Coins
body: Given N coin denominations and a target amount, print the fewest coins that sum exactly to the amount, or -1 if it cannot be made.
inputFormat: The first line contains N and the amount. The second line contains N space-separated denominations.
outputFormat: The minimum number of coins, or -1.

samples.explanation: 11 = 5 + 5 + 1 uses three coins.
No combination of 2s makes 3.

import sys
d = sys.stdin.read().split()
n, amt = int(d[0]), int(d[1])
coins = list(map(int, d[2:2+n]))
INF = float("inf")
dp = [0] + [INF] * amt
for v in range(1, amt + 1):
    for c in coins:
        if c <= v and dp[v - c] + 1 < dp[v]:
            dp[v] = dp[v - c] + 1
print(dp[amt] if dp[amt] != INF else -1)
editorial: Build up the best count for every amount from 1 to the target: each amount is one coin more than some smaller amount. Greedy fails here — with coins 1, 3 and 4, greedy makes 6 as 4+1+1 while 3+3 is better.
concept: Coin change is the standard example of a problem where greedy is wrong and DP is right.

title: Level Order Traversal Width
body: A binary tree is given as N nodes in level order, with -1 marking an absent child. Print the maximum number of nodes on any single level.

outputFormat: The largest number of real nodes on any level.

samples.explanation: The third level holds four nodes, the most of any level.
Each level holds at most one real node.

import sys

n = int(d[0])
a = d[1:1+n]
best = 0
level = 0
while (1 << level) - 1 < n:
    start = (1 << level) - 1

title: Shortest Path in Unweighted Grid
body: Given an R×C grid where 0 is open and 1 is blocked, print the fewest moves from the top-left to the bottom-right, moving up, down, left or right. Print -1 if unreachable.
inputFormat: The first line contains R and C. The next R lines each contain C characters.
outputFormat: The minimum number of moves, or -1.

samples.explanation: Going right, right, down, down takes four moves.
Both routes are blocked.

referencePython:
import sys
d = sys.stdin.read().split()
from collections import deque
r, c = int(d[0]), int(d[1])
g = d[2:2+r]
if g[0][0] == "1" or g[r-1][c-1] == "1":
    print(-1)
else:
    dist = [[-1]*c for _ in range(r)]
    dist[0][0] = 0
    q = deque([(0,0)])
    while q:
        x, y = q.popleft()
        for dx, dy in ((1,0),(-1,0),(0,1),(0,-1)):
            nx, ny = x+dx, y+dy
            if 0 <= nx < r and 0 <= ny < c and g[nx][ny] == "0" and dist[nx][ny] == -1:
                dist[nx][ny] = dist[x][y] + 1
                q.append((nx, ny))
    print(dist[r-1][c-1])
editorial: BFS explores in order of increasing distance, so the first time it reaches a cell it has done so in the fewest moves. That guarantee is exactly what makes BFS — not DFS — the right traversal for shortest paths on unweighted graphs.
concept: BFS layers the graph by hop count; DFS does not.

def sort(arr):

    if len(arr) < 2: return arr
    m = len(arr)//2
    l, r = sort(arr[:m]), sort(arr[m:])

    i = j = 0

    for mask in range(1 << n):
        sel = [acts[i] for i in range(n) if mask >> i & 1]
        sel.sort()
        ok = all(sel[i][1] <= sel[i+1][0] for i in range(len(sel)-1))
        if ok: best = max(best, len(sel))
    print(best)
concept: Greedy needs a proof; here it is an exchange argument on finish times.
hint: Which activity leaves the most time for everything after it?

title: Fractional Knapsack Value
body: Given N items with weights and values and a capacity W, print the maximum value obtainable when items may be taken fractionally. Print with three decimal places.
inputFormat: The first line contains N and W. Each of the next N lines contains a value and a weight.
outputFormat: The maximum value, to three decimal places.

samples.explanation: Take the first two whole and two thirds of the third, giving 240.000.
Half the item fits, giving 50.000.

referencePython:
import sys
d = sys.stdin.read().split()
n, w = int(d[0]), int(d[1])
items = [(int(d[2+2*i]), int(d[3+2*i])) for i in range(n)]
items.sort(key=lambda t: -t[0]/t[1])
total = 0.0
for v, wt in items:
    if w <= 0: break
    take = min(wt, w)
    total += v * take / wt
    w -= take
print(f"{total:.3f}")
editorial: Sorting by value per unit weight and filling greedily is optimal here precisely because items can be split — the last item is taken partially rather than being an all-or-nothing decision. The 0/1 version has no such greedy solution and needs dynamic programming.
concept: Divisibility is what makes greedy correct for fractional but not 0/1 knapsack.
hint: What changes if you cannot cut an item in half?

for v, wt in items:
    if cap <= 0: break
    if wt <= cap:
        total += v; cap -= wt
    else:
        total += v * (cap / wt); cap = 0
print(f"{total:.3f}")

title: Minimum Absolute Difference Pair
body: Print the smallest absolute difference between any two elements of an array.
inputFormat: The first line contains N. The second line contains N space-separated integers.

samples.explanation: 3 and 5 differ by 2, the smallest gap.
Only one pair exists.

referencePython:
import sys

a = sorted(map(int, d[1:1+n]))

editorial: After sorting, the closest pair must be adjacent — any non-adjacent pair has something between them, which is closer to at least one of the two. That reduces an O(n²) pairwise search to a single scan.

title: Longest Palindromic Substring Length
body: Print the length of the longest palindromic substring of S.
inputFormat: A single line containing the lowercase string S.
outputFormat: The length of the longest palindromic substring.

samples.explanation: "bab" and "aba" both have length 3.
"bb" has length 2.

editorial: Expand around every possible centre, of which there are 2n−1 — one per character and one between each adjacent pair, so that even-length palindromes are covered. That gives O(n²) time and O(1) space; Manacher’s algorithm reaches O(n) at considerably more complexity.
concept: Even-length palindromes need centres between characters, not just on them.
hint: Where is the centre of "bb"?

title: String Compression Run Length
body: Compress a string by replacing runs of the same character with the character followed by its count. If the result is not shorter, print the original.
inputFormat: A single line containing the lowercase string S.
outputFormat: The compressed string, or the original if compression does not shorten it.

samples.explanation: Runs give a2b1c5a3, which is shorter than the original.
Compression would give a1b1c1d1, which is longer, so the original is printed.

referencePython:
s = input().strip()
out = []
i = 0
while i < len(s):
    j = i
    while j < len(s) and s[j] == s[i]: j += 1
    out.append(s[i] + str(j - i))
    i = j
r = "".join(out)
print(r if len(r) < len(s) else s)
editorial: Walk the string counting each run. The final comparison matters: for a string with no repeats the compressed form is twice as long, so returning it would defeat the purpose. Building a list and joining once avoids the quadratic cost of repeated concatenation.
concept: A compression scheme that can expand its input needs a fallback.
hint: What does this scheme do to "abcd"?

title: Maximum Difference After Smaller
body: Print the maximum value of A[j] − A[i] where j > i, or -1 if no such pair gives a positive difference.
inputFormat: The first line contains N. The second line contains N space-separated integers.

samples.explanation: Buying at 1 and selling at 6 gives 5.
The array only falls, so no positive difference exists.

referencePython:
import sys
d = sys.stdin.read().split()
n = int(d[0])
a = list(map(int, d[1:1+n]))
low = a[0]
best = -1
for x in a[1:]:
    if x - low > 0: best = max(best, x - low)
    low = min(low, x)
print(best)
editorial: This is the single-transaction stock problem: track the smallest value seen so far and the best profit against it. One pass, O(1) space. Updating the minimum after computing the difference is what enforces j > i.
concept: Track the best candidate so far rather than revisiting earlier elements.
hint: What is the best you could have bought at before today?

title: Zigzag Level Sum
body: A binary tree is given in level order with -1 for absent nodes. Print the sum of values on the deepest level containing at least one real node.
inputFormat: The first line contains N. The second line contains N space-separated values in level order.
outputFormat: The sum of the deepest level with real nodes.

samples.explanation: The deepest occupied level holds 4 and 5, summing to 9.
Only the root exists.

referencePython:
import sys
d = sys.stdin.read().split()
n = int(d[0])
a = d[1:1+n]
best_level = -1
total = 0
level = 0
while (1 << level) - 1 < n:
    start = (1 << level) - 1
    end = min(start + (1 << level), n)
    vals = [int(a[i]) for i in range(start, end) if a[i] != "-1"]
    if vals:
        best_level = level; total = sum(vals)
    level += 1
print(total)
editorial: Walk the levels using their index ranges, remembering the sum of the last one that contained a real node. On a linked tree the same result comes from a BFS that overwrites the running sum at each new level.
concept: The last non-empty level is found by remembering, not by searching backwards.
hint: What do you keep as you move down the levels?

title: Number of Provinces
body: Given an N×N adjacency matrix of 0s and 1s, print how many connected groups of cities it contains.
inputFormat: The first line contains N. The next N lines each contain N characters.

samples.explanation: Cities 1 and 2 are connected; city 3 is alone.
All three are connected.

referencePython:
import sys
d = sys.stdin.read().split()
n = int(d[0])
g = d[1:1+n]
seen = [False]*n
c = 0
for i in range(n):
    if seen[i]: continue
    c += 1
    st = [i]; seen[i] = True
    while st:
        u = st.pop()
        for v in range(n):
            if g[u][v] == "1" and not seen[v]:
                seen[v] = True; st.append(v)
print(c)
editorial: Counting connected components: start a traversal from each unvisited city and mark everything reachable. The number of traversals started is the number of provinces. Union-Find solves the same problem and is preferable when edges arrive incrementally.
concept: One traversal per unvisited node counts components.
hint: How many times do you need to start a fresh search?

title: Sum of Subarray Minimums
body: Print the sum over all contiguous subarrays of the minimum element of each, modulo 1000000007.
inputFormat: The first line contains N. The second line contains N space-separated positive integers.
outputFormat: The sum of subarray minimums, modulo 1000000007.

samples.explanation: The subarray minimums add up to 17.
The only subarray is the element itself.

referencePython:
import sys
d = sys.stdin.read().split()
M = 10**9 + 7
n = int(d[0])
a = list(map(int, d[1:1+n]))
left = [0]*n
right = [0]*n
st = []
for i in range(n):
    while st and a[st[-1]] > a[i]: st.pop()
    left[i] = i - (st[-1] if st else -1)
    st.append(i)
st = []
for i in range(n-1, -1, -1):
    while st and a[st[-1]] >= a[i]: st.pop()
    right[i] = (st[-1] if st else n) - i
    st.append(i)
print(sum(a[i]*left[i]*right[i] for i in range(n)) % M)
editorial: Rather than enumerating subarrays, count how many have each element as their minimum: the number of choices to the left times the number to the right, bounded by the nearest smaller element on each side. Using strict comparison on one side and non-strict on the other is what stops equal values being counted twice.

title: Word Break Feasible
body: Given a string S and a dictionary of N words, print YES if S can be segmented into a sequence of dictionary words, otherwise NO.
inputFormat: The first line contains S. The second line contains N. The next N lines each contain a word.

samples.explanation: "leet" plus "code" covers the whole string.

samples.input:
catsandog
5
cats
dog
sand
and
cat
samples.explanation: No segmentation reaches the end.

referencePython:
import sys
lines = [l for l in sys.stdin.read().split("\n")]
s = lines[0].strip()
n = int(lines[1])
words = set(lines[2:2+n])
m = len(s)
dp = [False]*(m+1)
dp[0] = True
for i in range(1, m+1):
    for j in range(i):
        if dp[j] and s[j:i] in words:
            dp[i] = True; break
print("YES" if dp[m] else "NO")
editorial: dp[i] records whether the first i characters can be segmented. It is true when some earlier valid split point j leaves a dictionary word between j and i. The greedy approach of taking the longest matching word fails on "aaa" with dictionary {"aa"}, which is why this needs DP.
concept: Segmentation problems need every split point considered, not just the greedy one.
hint: Try "aaa" with only the word "aa" available.
